If you translate wildcard to a capturing group, the expectation should be that only that group is being replaced during compilation:

```js
const pattern = new URLPattern("/images/*.jpg");
pattern.generate('pathname', ['1']) // "images/1.jpg"
```

I'd treat wildcards as non-named pattern segments, implying that the way they are compiled is the same as for the named segments. The only difference is the compilation input:

```js
// This is a named equivalent of the wildcard example above.
const pattern = new URLPattern("/images/:filename.jpg");
pattern.generate('pathname', { filename: "1" }) // "images/1.jpg"
```

Replacing a fixed portion of the pattern (".jpg") would be unexpected.
Wildcards are unnamed matching groups today.  So they do indeed get an automatically assigned numeric name.

I was mainly addressing the comment from @Jamesernator in regards to the ambiguous match of `*.jpg`. I think the expectation is to have only the asterisk replaced, just as the expectation is that only a named parameter is replaced (`:name.jpg`). I think this may not be a concern.

Just would like to chime in that this is very important, and that I can’t imagine a case where you read urls into objects without also turning objects into urls. Search pages for example have lots of generated links (think filters, pagination), but also read the url into local state.

I were just merely considering if a result could be mutable...
for example: Say that you are on `shopify.com/categories/computers` and want to navigate to games section `shopify.com/categories/games`

```js
const pattern = new URLPattern({ pathname: ':vendor/categories/:category' })
// Get current url pattern
const result = pattern.exec(location.href)

result.pathname.groups.category = 'games' // Modify current url match result
location.href = result.toString() // change the url location
```
Thinking this could be useful for a adv search with 2 way data binding or something.

all doe a `generate` function could work as equally good, maybe mutable url pattern result isn't desirable?

the pattern being mutable can make sense, as new URL is a precedence, but personally I would need to make a copy of the pattern for every change then, as you have many links with different state, as it's not the current state you want to show in the URL, but a possible future state

Would be helpful for my use case. I use a URL pattern to 

1. determine type of page
2. extract information from the url
3. reconstruct the URL from extracted information

I'm sure this will be a common enough use case for URLPattern

This API is highly benefitial for i18n/localization where localized URLs have to be mapped back to the original (deLocalized) URL. Here are docs for the use case that should be accounted for https://inlang.com/m/gerre34r/library-inlang-paraglideJs/strategy#url.

I feel it's better to expose this API to the [URLPattern](https://urlpattern.spec.whatwg.org/#urlpattern) interface, rather than making it mutable with adding `toString()` in [URLPatternResult](https://urlpattern.spec.whatwg.org/#dictdef-urlpatternresult), which is currently defined as dictionary and doesn't have any method.

Will it make sense to pass a record to generate to deal with the complete URL?
JavaScript code example might be something like:
```
const pattern = URLPattern("https://example.com/:path");
const result = await pattern.generate({'path': 'image/a.jpg'});
const generatedURL = result.toString();  // expecting "https://example.com/image/a.jpg"
```

What do you think?

> fyi, the reference library only supports pathname to generate a string tho. https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp#compile-reverse-path-to-regexp
> 
> I'm wondering how we should handle the case if there are two named groups which have the same name?

Yeah, applying it other than pathnames sounds challenging.
Is it realistic to limit the generate application only within the pathname field? 

> const pattern = new URLPattern('https://{:pattern.}?example.com/:pattern');
> const result = await pattern.generate({'pattern': 'image/a.jpg'});
> // => ???
> It looks the current design doesn't have a capability to substitute two strings which have same names in a different component.

Even if it is useless, I feel it natural to generate `{'protocol': 'https', 'hostname': 'image/a.jpgexample.com', 'pathname': /image/a.jpg`,...}`.  It should be a web developer's responsibility to avoid practically unusable cases.

For the IFT use case the set of variables is fixed and have well defined values (base32/base64 encodings) so it would pretty unusual for IFT template to substitute one of the variables outside of the path or query string.

Does anyone have ideas for how to handle input strings with _delimiter chars_ (e.g. `/` in pathname) ?

For segment-wildcard parts, whether encoding delimiter chars or not affects whether the generated string matches the original pattern or not.
```javascript
const p1 = new URLPattern({ pathname: "/:id" });
const s1 = p1.generate("pathname", { id: "aaa/bbb" });  // should return "/aaa/bbb" or "/aaa%2Fbbb" ?
p1.test("https://example.com/" + s1);  // returns `false` if "/aaa/bbb", `true` otherwise
```
I personally think that the encoding option is better.

However, for full-wildcard parts, it may be confusing to encode input strings. 
```javascript
const p2 = new URLPattern({ pathname: "/posts/*/edit" });
const s2 = p2.generate("pathname", { 0: "2025/04/01" });
// should return "/posts/2025/04/01/edit" or "/posts/2025%2F04%2F01/edit" ?
```
In this case, my intuition is that `s2` should be `/posts/2025/04/01/edit`, but I am not confident enough.

The current Chrome experimental implementation throws TypeError when one of the input strings has the delimiter chars.
I agree with both of your intuitions. I guess the second example is hard though if you are not yet doing full-wildcards.

Thanks! As of full-wildcards, I have a slight concern that I have also mentioned in [a DesignDoc comment](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ca6geyHD40MfHkalgEv4AcBo9-rHK6CrAOxwcWor9WA/edit?usp=drivesdk&disco=AAABfmqmQtI): using numeric name to specify full-wildcards may be confusing.
For example, the full-wildcard in `/(abc)/*` has the numeric name `1` per implicit naming in the parsing step ([add-a-part algorithm](https://urlpattern.spec.whatwg.org/#add-a-part)), but some people expect it to have the name `0`.

I see, because `(abc)` gets position 0, right?

Let me recap my understanding of the current situation:

1. `generate()` on a URLPattern with segment-wildcard parts and non-delimiter inputs will work
1. `generate()` on a URLPattern with segment-wildcard parts and delimiter inputs will throw
1. `generate()` on a URLPattern with regexp/full-wildcard parts and non-delimiter inputs will throw
1. `generate()` on a URLPattern with regexp/full-wildcard parts and delimiter inputs will throw

If this is correct, I think changing (2) from throw to encode is fine. And we retain optionality on how to change the behavior of (3) and (4) in the future.

@domenic You are right. `(abc)` gets position 0, and the current situation is exactly as you summed up. (Sorry if I confused you.)

I am for your idea and still need ideas on (3) and (4). Thanks for sorting out!

It would be great if there was a platform primitive for substituting values into URLs that could be used by HTML elements and scripting applications alike - off the top of my head, similar to how `media` attribute and `matchMedia` API may work (I think). 

I think it could be useful for applications other than maps.  But it's definitely useful in maps for embedding fetches for tiles, images and other 2D-covering resources.  Maybe it would be useful in 3D as well, who knows.  Happy to discuss anytime.

Yes, what I meant was that what you're going to build in URLPattern.generate might not only be available to scripting in the platform, but also be available as a feature used by HTML elements / attributes, similar to how (I imagine) the underlying code for the `matchMedia` API may be used by the `media` attribute. 

In MapML, we have used URI level 1 template syntax to associate a named input to a template variable.  The values of the variables created by the inputs are replaced into the template when required by the application, and the resource is then fetched at the created URL.  Here is the polyfill markup that we are using. We are open to using the URLPattern.generate approach and syntax if that is the chosen direction for the browser platform.

Here is a map extent marked up currently using URI template syntax for variables:

```html
    <map-extent units="OSMTILE" checked="checked" hidden="hidden">
      <map-input name="z" type="zoom" value="0" min="0" max="18"></map-input>
      <map-input name="x" type="location" units="tilematrix" axis="column" min="0" max="1"></map-input>
      <map-input name="y" type="location" units="tilematrix" axis="row" min="0" max="1"></map-input>
      <map-link rel="tile" tref="https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"></map-link>
    </map-extent>
```

The {z}/{x}/{y} URI template syntax above has the benefit of being familiar to many people.

I could see this becoming something like the following, if I understand your explainer correctly:

```html
    <map-extent units="OSMTILE" checked="checked" hidden="hidden">
      <map-input name="z" type="zoom" value="0" min="0" max="18"></map-input>
      <map-input name="x" type="location" units="tilematrix" axis="column" min="0" max="1"></map-input>
      <map-input name="y" type="location" units="tilematrix" axis="row" min="0" max="1"></map-input>
      <map-link rel="tile" hrefpattern="https://tile.openstreetmap.org/:z/:x/:y.png"></map-link>
    </map-extent>
```

another example (of potential URLPattern use)

```html
    <map-extent units="OSMTILE" checked>
      <map-input name="w" type="width"></map-input>
      <map-input name="h" type="height"></map-input>
      <map-input name="xmin" type="location" units="pcrs" position="top-left" axis="easting"></map-input>
      <map-input name="ymin" type="location" units="pcrs" position="bottom-left" axis="northing"></map-input>
      <map-input name="xmax" type="location" units="pcrs" position="top-right" axis="easting"></map-input>
      <map-input name="ymax" type="location" units="pcrs" position="top-left" axis="northing"></map-input>
      <!-- Web Map Service URLPattern requesting whole-map images -->
      <map-link rel="image" hrefpattern="https://wms.ess-ws.nrcan.gc.ca/wms/toporama_en?SERVICE=WMS&REQUEST=GetMap&FORMAT=image/jpeg&TRANSPARENT=FALSE&STYLES=&VERSION=1.3.0&LAYERS=WMS-Toporama&WIDTH=:w&HEIGHT=:h&CRS=EPSG:3857&BBOX=:xmin,:ymin,:xmax,:ymax"></map-link>
    </map-extent>
```
I wonder if the presence of ":" in "EPSG:3857" in the above hrefpattern would be problematic?  It doesn't represent a variable for substitution, it's part of the string content of the URL that's required by the server's CRS parameter value.

> I wonder if the presence of ":" in "EPSG:3857" in the above hrefpattern would be problematic? It doesn't represent a variable for substitution, it's part of the string content of the URL that's required by the server's CRS parameter value.

Yes, IIUC, the ":" in strings should be escaped. For example, `"EPSG:3857"` should be encoded as `"EPSG\\:3857"` for URLPattern.

I'm a little confused because I'm seeing two different use cases that don't use the same API here. One use case is to *execute* a `URLPattern` against a URL, modify the `URLPatternResult`, and (re)serialize/stringify the result back into a URL.

This is what @jimmywarting discussed.

> I were just merely considering if a result could be mutable... for example: Say that you are on `shopify.com/categories/computers` and want to navigate to games section `shopify.com/categories/games`
> 
> const pattern = new URLPattern({ pathname: ':vendor/categories/:category' })
> // Get current url pattern
> const result = pattern.exec(location.href)
> 
> result.pathname.groups.category = 'games' // Modify current url match result
> location.href = result.toString() // change the url location
> 
> Thinking this could be useful for a adv search with 2 way data binding or something.
> 
> all doe a `generate` function could work as equally good, maybe mutable url pattern result isn't desirable?

The second use case is to take a URLPattern and fill in the pattern's parameters to make a URL or URL component. This is what @azaika and @sisidovski cover in the proposed https://github.com/explainers-by-googlers/urlpattern-generate API. *This is also I believe the original focus of this thread, as per the starting comment:*

> One of the most frequent pieces of feedback we have gotten is that developers would like to generate URL and component strings from a URLPattern. For example, something like:
> 
> const pattern = new URLPattern({ pathname: '/product/:id' });
> const my_pathname = pattern.generate('pathname', { id: '12345' });
> // my_pathname is "/product/12345"

Would it make sense to create a new issue here to split out the first use case about modifying and serializing `URLPatternResult`s? Please correct me if I'm missing some part of this thread :)

I think you are correct that from a developer's perspective, both approaches serve the same high-level goal: obtaining a URL string from a pattern.

Rather than seeing them as two different use cases, I view them as two distinct approaches to solve that single goal.

* Stateless Generation: Filling in parameters directly via URLPattern.generate().
* Stateful Transformation: Executing a pattern, modifying the URLPatternResult, and re-serializing it.

As I mentioned earlier, the second approach is technically more challenging because URLPatternResult is currently defined as a dictionary and lacks methods.

But do you have any concrete use case that doesn't work with the stateless approach but work with the stateful approach?
How would the example I quoted for the first use case be solved by the proposed `generate' API?
